patch.value: ADR: one release per UTC day is architectural, not a policy gate - decide whether a manually triggered same-day release is a supported operation

Live verification 2026-07-31: the scheduled Auto Release run at 05:50:49Z succeeded, v2026.7.31 is the latest GitHub release, npm dist-tag latest resolves 2026.7.31, and both npx @unbrained/pm-cli@latest and bunx @unbrained/pm-cli@2026.7.31 report 2026.7.31. One release per day is working end to end on both package runners. The Auto Release workflow's issues:closed trigger is correctly fenced by its job-level if to the specific bot-authored blocker issue, and the four issue-triggered runs today all report skipped.

The open question is what should happen on a deliberate second release in one day, because two independent mechanisms currently forbid it and only one of them is a policy.

The policy gate is maybeSkipForSameDayRelease in scripts/release/run-release-pipeline.mjs:263-279, which lists local tags matching v<todayKey>* and skips with reason release_already_cut_today. It is evaluated unconditionally at line 423, so workflow_dispatch is gated exactly as the schedule is, and --allow-same-day-release was deliberately removed at lines 384-387 with the message directing operators to retry the existing tag through the Release workflow.

The architectural constraint is resolveVersion at lines 103-112, which fails unless the target version equals the current UTC date key. A second release on the same day would need a second distinct version, and the date-based scheme has no room for one: 2026.7.31 is already published and npm will not accept a re-publish. So even removing the policy gate would not enable a second same-day release; it would produce a version collision.

The stated intent - never two automatic releases per day unless manually triggered - is therefore not satisfiable today, and the gap is in the version grammar rather than in the guard. Three options, and this decision should pick one rather than leaving the intent and the implementation disagreeing.

First, ratify the current behaviour: one release per UTC day, full stop, with a partial failure recovered by retrying the existing tag rather than cutting a new version. This is what the code does and what the removal message already assumes; it costs nothing and makes the guard's unconditional evaluation correct by design rather than by accident.

Second, add a same-day ordinal: 2026.7.31.1 for the second cut of the day. This satisfies the stated intent, and it changes the version grammar everywhere it is parsed or compared - scripts/sync-versions.mjs, the padded-versus-unpadded comparison that once silently skipped releases, the changelog release-tag matching, plugin and marketplace manifests, and any consumer pinning a caret range. The cost is broad and the benefit narrow.

Third, keep one version per day and allow a manual re-run to amend the same version before it is published, which covers the real operational need - a same-day fix after a bad cut - without a new version at all.

The recommendation is the first option, with the third as the documented recovery path, because the operational need is amendment rather than a second release. Whichever is chosen, the guard's behaviour under workflow_dispatch should be stated in docs/RELEASING.md, since an operator today sees a manual dispatch skip with no explanation of why manual and scheduled behave identically.

One option is accepted and recorded in this decision with its rationale, and the rejected options are retained with the reason so the question is not reopened from scratch; docs/RELEASING.md states what a manual workflow_dispatch does when a release already exists for the current UTC day, and names the supported recovery path for a partial failure; If the ratify option is accepted, the unconditional evaluation of the same-day guard is documented as intentional at the call site so it is not later read as a bug and made dispatch-conditional; If the ordinal option is accepted, every version-parsing and version-comparison site is enumerated before any change lands, including the padded-versus-unpadded comparison that previously skipped releases silently; The decision records the live verification captured here - one successful scheduled run, one release, npm latest and both npx and bunx resolving it - as the baseline the policy is being decided against

value.text:
Evidence base attached 2026-07-31. This decision was reachable from its capability parent and from the GA milestone, but from none of the six items that measure the thing it rules on, so a graph walk from the ADR could not find the evidence and a walk from any defect could not find the ADR.

What the attached items establish, and why each bears on the ruling rather than merely sharing a topic:

pm-ki67py is the guard itself, and it is now recorded as blocked_by this decision because the defect admits two different correct repairs depending on which way this rules. That is the sharpest reason to decide: the fix cannot be written until the ruling exists.

pm-44u3wt establishes that all 84 scheduled runs fired 2.5-4 hours after the declared cron time. The cron in .github/workflows/auto-release.yml is 35 2 * * *, so the effective release instant is roughly 05:00-06:30 UTC. A one-release-per-UTC-day rule whose trigger sits within a few hours of a UTC boundary is a rule whose day assignment is decided by queue latency. If this decision keeps the UTC day as the unit, it should say what happens when drift pushes a run across midnight, because that is the case that produces either two releases in one calendar day or none.

pm-e70zh5 establishes a 32-of-84 failure rate. That matters here because the retry path is the only mechanism that can produce a same-day second attempt, so a chronically failing scheduled path is precisely the condition that exercises the question this ADR is asking.

pm-q91qyd establishes that the three release ledgers disagree in both directions - six published npm artifacts with no changelog section, seven git tags never published. A one-per-day invariant is only checkable against a ledger that agrees with itself; whichever ledger this decision names as authoritative for what already released that day is a substantive part of the ruling, not an implementation detail.

pm-lpqln4 and pm-u0oz2k establish that the post-publish verification cannot currently prove a release works: the bunx probe accepts an inert token, and the pm-mcp entrypoint is never executed at all. They bear on this decision because a same-day manual re-release is a recovery operation, and a recovery path is only worth authorising if the pipeline can tell a recovered release from a broken one.

value.author: harness:codex
value.text: Maintainer decision input 2026-08-03: there must never be two automatic releases in one day; a second same-day release is permissible only when explicitly manually triggered. The ADR should formalize separate automatic and manual semantics, immutable trigger provenance, ordinal or alternative version rules for the manual exception, and a gate proving scheduled or issue-retry execution can never consume that exception.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Decision input recorded 2026-08-07 — maintainer intent, stated directly.

The maintainer's stated requirement is: there should never be two automatic releases per UTC day, but a manually triggered release is expected to be a supported operation. That is a ruling on the open question in this item's title, and it splits the guard the pipeline currently implements.

What the pipeline does today, verified against the source and against three real runs on 2026-08-07. The guard lists tags for the current UTC date key and, if any exists, writes a skip receipt with reason release_already_cut_today. It reads no trigger information, so it applies identically to a scheduled run and to a workflow_dispatch. The removed --allow-same-day-release flag has an explicit refusal directing the operator to retry the existing tag through the Release workflow instead. Today's sequence exercised it end to end: the 04:36Z scheduled run failed on the production-error gate, a 10:12Z dispatch cut v2026.8.7, and a 10:24Z dispatch skipped on the guard. One release for the day across three runs, which is the correct outcome for that sequence and says nothing about the question this item asks, because the second dispatch was a recovery retry rather than a deliberate second release.

The gap between the stated intent and the implementation is therefore narrow and precise: the guard is trigger-blind, so honouring the intent requires the pipeline to distinguish schedule from dispatch, which it currently never reads.

The architectural objection this item exists to weigh is unchanged and must be answered before the guard is relaxed. The version scheme is the calendar date. A second release on the same date has no stable version to occupy: an ordinal suffix is a prerelease under the ranges that downstream packages declare, and the release-version script already refuses on exactly that ground. So "manual same-day release is supported" cannot be satisfied by relaxing the guard alone; it requires either a version scheme with same-day ordinality that still satisfies stable peer ranges, or an explicit statement that a manual same-day release means republishing the existing date version rather than cutting a new one.

Those are the two dispositions this ADR should choose between, and they are genuinely different products. Framing them so the decision is a ruling rather than a discussion:

Disposition one, retry semantics. A manual trigger on a date that already has a tag means "finish or repeat the release for this date", not "cut another". The guard stays date-based, the dispatch path routes to the existing tag, and the refusal text — which already says this — becomes the contract rather than an error message. Nothing changes in the version scheme. The cost is that a maintainer who genuinely wants a second distinct release on one day cannot have one.

Disposition two, ordinal same-day releases. The version scheme gains a same-day component and every consumer range, sync script, and compatibility matrix absorbs it. This is a real product change with a wide blast radius, and it is worth doing only if a second distinct same-day release is a use case someone actually has, which no recorded evidence in this tracker currently demonstrates.

Recommendation carried into the ADR, not asserted as decided: disposition one satisfies the maintainer's stated intent — manual triggering is supported, and it is exactly the recovery operation the pipeline already performs — without touching the version scheme, and it makes the trigger-blindness a documented property rather than an accident. Disposition two should stay open only if a concrete need for two distinct same-day releases is recorded here as evidence.

value.text: Maintainer directive recorded 2026-08-08: the stated requirement is that there must never be two AUTO releases in one UTC day unless a release is manually triggered. The first half is satisfied today and provably so — listTodayTags compares parsed year/month/day components rather than a prefix glob, so the guard cannot mis-skip or double-cut. The second half is still exactly this decision's open question, because the guard is trigger-blind: a workflow_dispatch run hits the same release_already_cut_today skip as the 02:35 cron, and --allow-same-day-release was deliberately removed with the rationale that a partial failure should be retried through the Release workflow against the existing tag rather than by minting a second same-day version. Not re-adding the override as a drive-by, since its removal was an explicit prior decision and re-introducing a second same-day version path is a semantics change to release automation. What this needs is a ruling between two coherent options: keep one version per UTC day architectural and treat the existing-tag retry as the only manual path, or make the skip trigger-aware so workflow_dispatch may mint an ordinal same-day version. The directive is evidence for the second, and pm-db8onn's stale-tag rerun behaviour is the concrete cost of the first.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Decision input from the maintainer, 2026-08-10, restating the intent verbatim: the daily auto release must run whenever changes have happened since the last release, and there must never be two AUTO-releases in one day unless a release is manually triggered.

This resolves the ambiguity the ADR flagged but does not by itself pick an option, because the sentence contains two clauses that this ADR has already shown land on different mechanisms.

The first clause is satisfied today. The scheduled path cuts at most one release per UTC day, enforced twice over - by maybeSkipForSameDayRelease and, independently, by resolveVersion refusing any version that is not the current UTC date key. Nothing needs to change for the automatic half of the intent to hold, and the double enforcement is why it has held.

The second clause is the live question. 'Unless manually triggered' asks for a deliberate same-day release to be a supported operation, and that is exactly what is unavailable: the guard is trigger-blind at line 423, so workflow_dispatch is gated identically to schedule, and even lifting that gate only moves the failure to a version collision, since 2026.8.10 would already be published.

So the maintainer's intent selects option two, the same-day ordinal, over option one, ratifying one-per-day. Recording that the intent points there rather than declaring the ADR accepted, because option two is the expensive branch: it changes the version grammar in every place a version is parsed, compared, or synchronised, including the padded-versus-unpadded comparison that has previously skipped releases silently, and that blast radius deserves its own accepted decision rather than being inherited from a sentence.

What would make this safely decidable: enumerate every consumer of the version grammar and state, per consumer, whether a three-segment date key with a trailing ordinal parses and orders correctly. The comparison bug in the record is the reason to enumerate rather than assume.

patch.value: A scheduled or issue-triggered automatic path can publish at most one version for a UTC date, with a negative control that a second automatic attempt skips before version mutation; An explicit workflow_dispatch after the daily release can mint the next stable YYYY.M.D-N follow-up and records immutable manual-trigger provenance; Every version parser, comparator, synchronizer, changelog grouper, package range, plugin manifest, release verifier, npm check, npx probe, and bunx probe is inventoried and covered for base and ordinal forms; Concurrent manual dispatches allocate one ordinal without collision or duplicate publication; Partial-release recovery distinguishes retrying the existing version from requesting a distinct follow-up; docs/RELEASING.md states the two paths and their exact receipts; focused tests plus the full local and hosted release gates prove npm, npx, Bun, and bunx behavior without publishing during validation

The accepted calendar-versioning ADR pm-ee1k already defines YYYY.M.D for the first UTC-day release, YYYY.M.D-N for explicit manual follow-ups, and at most one automatic release per day. The current pipeline drifted from that decision: its same-day guard is trigger-blind and its resolver rejects the ordinal version, so this item now owns restoring the accepted behavior, enumerating every version consumer, and proving automatic triggers cannot consume the manual exception.
Restore accepted manual same-day follow-up releases while preserving one automatic release per UTC day

value.text: Live verification 2026-08-16: the guard is confirmed trigger-blind at scripts/release/run-release-pipeline.mjs:475. maybeSkipForSameDayRelease is called unconditionally in the main path, before any event-source branch, so a workflow_dispatch run on a day that already has a tag skips with reason release_already_cut_today exactly as a scheduled run does. listTodayTags compares parsed year/month/day components rather than a prefix glob, so the unpadded-date false positive is not in play. The one-automatic-release-per-UTC-day property this item must preserve is therefore currently held by the same predicate that also blocks the accepted manual follow-up, which is the whole of the remaining work here: the skip needs an event-source-aware branch, not a different date computation. Today's scheduled run (databaseId 31924312921) succeeded and produced v2026.8.16; npm dist-tag latest is 2026.8.16; npx and bunx both resolve and execute 2026.8.16.

value.text:
Re-verified 2026-08-30 at e3897a319, and one detail has changed in a way that could mislead a later reader.

.github/workflows/auto-release.yml now guards its 'Detect immutable same-day automatic target' step with if: github.event_name != 'workflow_dispatch'. That is a workflow-level step guard covering provenance detection and the build-skip chain, and it is easy to read as the trigger-awareness this item asks for. It is not. The pipeline-level guard is unchanged: maybeSkipForSameDayRelease at scripts/release/run-release-pipeline.mjs:312 still takes only (tagsToday, todayKey, outputJson), carries no event or trigger parameter, and is called unconditionally at line 475 before any event-source branch. A workflow_dispatch run on a day that already carries a tag therefore still skips with release_already_cut_today.

So the property this item must preserve is confirmed held, and the property it exists to restore is confirmed still absent.

Automatic-path evidence for today: the scheduled run 33301745849 at 08:30:20Z succeeded and cut exactly one v2026.8.30; GitHub shows a single release for the date, and the five preceding tags v2026.8.26 through v2026.8.30 are one per UTC day. npm dist-tags.latest is 2026.8.30. npx -y @unbrained/pm-cli@latest and bunx @unbrained/pm-cli@latest both print 2026.8.30 from a directory outside the repository, so neither resolves the local build.

No change made here: making the pipeline guard trigger-aware without the ordinal version work would let a manual dispatch mint a second release for the same date under the base YYYY.M.D identity, which is the collision this item's acceptance criteria are written to prevent.
